newsitem.title: UK: US nuclear fusion facility shut by budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: US nuclear fusion facility shut by budget cuts.

text.p: A $1.5 billion device holding the world record for controlled nuclear fusion was mothballed this month because of budget cuts, U.S. officials said on Friday.
"The final experiment happened last Friday," said Tony DeMeo, a spokesman for the Tokamak Fusion Test Reactor (TFTR) at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory at Princeton, New Jersey.
"The biggest factor has been the need to cut the federal deficit."
The doughnut-shaped reactor was closed because of a reduction in the U.S. fusion energy research budget, which has fallen to around $225 million this year from some $360 million in 1995, he said.

Building work began on the TFTR in 1977 and it stands alongside the Joint European Torus (JET) in England in having produced controlled nuclear fusion - the process which creates the energy of the sun and the hydrogen bomb.

Scientists say that while expensive, fusion technology could provide in the next century a source of energy with an almost limitless supply of fuel, with few of the dangers associated with nuclear fission and none of the environmentally damaging emissions of conventional fossil fuel-burning power stations.
TFTR produced 10.7 megawatts of power for one second in 1994, which still stands as a world record. Officials at JET hope to achieve, and surpass this, later this year.
The TFTR device cost around $1.5 billion to build in today's dollars, and running costs have been around $40 million on an annual basis, DeMeo said.

This compares with annual civilian world nuclear fusion research costs of around $1.1 billion, according to 1995 data released by the International Energy Agency. This figure represents a fall in real terms of almost 30 percent since 1985.

The project is coordinated with other fusion research programmes around the world which are expected to lead to the construction of the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) which is expected to attain the physicists' goal of ignition - when the energy produced by the reaction is sufficient to sustain the process.
ITER is expected to reach 1,500 megawatts for perhaps 15 minutes. After that there are plans for a commercial reactor which is not likely to be ready before 2025 at the earliest.
The TFTR will be mothballed although there are no immediate plans for it to be dismantled, DeMeo said.

Work at the laboratory will now focus on a smaller device, the National Spherical Torus Experiment (NSTX) which will cost $20 million to build and use $130 million worth of existing infrastructure, he said.
Further cuts are planned -- the budget for the laboratory will be cut to $47.6 million in 1998 from $56 million this financial year.
Around 150-200 people are expected to be laid off at Princeton because of the latest shutdown.
"The tragedy is in the loss of human resources. They had some ideas they wanted to test and these are now going to have to wait for ITER, which is at least ten years away," DeMeo said.
"When we finally realise there is an energy crisis we will need an alternative."
